newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Riot at Bulgarian parliament blocks new government.
newsitem.headline: Riot at Bulgarian parliament blocks new government.

text.p: Riot engulfed Bulgaria's parliament on Friday, preventing the appointment of a new Socialist government.
Anti-government protesters stormed the building. Opposition deputies demanding a general election declared first a sit-in, then a boycott.

President Zhelyu Zhelev, returning from a trip to France, dropped plans to appoint a new prime minister on Saturday from the ruling Socialists, who are in the middle of an economic crisis and a leadership upheaval. He called a meeting of the advisory National Security Council instead.
"I back the protests of the people, who have been driven to this humiliating state," Zhelev, who is normally a figurehead and has less than two weeks left in office, declared on national television.
"In this way they are demonstrating their dignity," he said, but added: "I do not approve of violence and appeal for order."
Dozens of demonstrators forced their way into the parliament building late on Friday afternoon.
Police fought them back, spraying them with tear gas and water and barricading the corridors with tables and chairs.
Some 50,000 people massed outside blowing whistles and burning red flags and effigies representing the Socialist Party.
All windows were smashed on the ground floor of the building, a Renaissance-style landmark in the centre of Sofia.
Police trained jets of water down on to crowds who were smashing and overturning the cars which deputies had parked outside.

President-elect Petar Stoyanov -- an opposition figure whose election two months ago marked the collapse of public support for the Socialists -- was overcome by teargas while trying to calm the crowd. He was taken away by bodyguards.

Some 200 Interior Ministry troops were brought in to guard the doors of parliament but Socialist deputies dared not leave and opposition members declared they would stay until the Socialists agreed to an election.
The opposition deputies later left, saying they feared for the safety of the demonstrators outside.
"We will start preparations for a nationwide political strike and we believe everyone will join us," said Ivan Kostov chairman of the Union of Democratic Forces, the main oposition party.
"After this clash and this lack of understanding, we believe there is no possibility for us to stay and keep on working in this parliament."
Ambulances took away protesters and policemen who collapsed from tear gas. One hospital said it was treating 15 injured with more still arriving.
Demonstrators blocked narrow streets nearby and pelted any Socialist deputy who tried to step outside with chunks of ice.
People were bringing hot drinks and food for the opposition supporters. Nearby art galleries handed out free coffee and tea.

The government issued an appeal for calm, urging citizens "not to give way to provocations in the name of preserving social peace." The Interior Ministry called for dialogue to resolve tensions but said it would do everything necessary "within the law".
"I hope there is enough common sense not to impose a state of emergency," said Union of Democratic Forces deputy Filip Dimitrov, a former prime minister .
A quarter of Bulgaria's banks are in receivership and triple-digit inflation has slashed real incomes.
On Wednesday the Socialists nominated Interior Minister Nikolai Dobrev, the party's strongman, as prime minister in place of Zhan Videnov, who resigned unexectedly on December 21.
Dobrev was prevented from leaving parliament on Friday by a volley of snowballs.
The opposition says the Socialists have failed to tackle the economic crisis and now lack support to form a government.
Voters delivered a powerful no-confidence vote two months ago by electing opposition candidate Stoyanov as president with a 60 percent majority.
The lev collapsed at 660 to the dollar on Friday, from 70 a year ago. It has lost 35 percent of its value against the dollar since the beginning of the year.
"The BSP which led the country to its gravest crisis in history has no right to rule," said Yordan Sokolov, parliamentary leader of the Union of Democratic Forces.

As soon as parliament approve a new cabinet the International Monetary Fund plans to negotiate implementaton of a tough fixed exchange regime as a last resort to restore confidence in the crumbling economy.
